title: Latency degradation scenarios and runbook design
summary: Working session to map out plausible latency-degradation scenarios, decide on automatic fallback priorities, and draft a short runbook for on-call and release engineers. We validated assumptions around KV cache warm-up, batching trade-offs, and a proposed two-tier fallback (quantized variant then model fallback). Agreed immediate action items: add a prewarming signal to the scheduler, document p99 vs p95 rollback thresholds, and schedule an end-to-end benchmark with representative workloads.
topics: Scenario mapping: causes of slow tokens (KV cache misses, compaction, OOM, network egress)
Fallback policy ordering and scoring (latency vs cost vs quality)
Runbook structure: detection, triage, mitigation, communication
Telemetry gaps: p99 traces, cold-start tagging, kernel-fallback metrics
Rollout gating: canary thresholds and automatic rollback triggers
action_items: Darius Chen: Add prewarm signal to scheduler + spike test (due 2026-11-25)
Priya Kapoor: Prototype two-tier fallback logic in staging and add unit tests (due 2026-11-30)
Mateo Ruiz: Instrument KV cache miss reason codes and log sampling (due 2026-11-22)
Aisha Thompson: Create regression suite for latency-degradation scenarios (due 2026-12-02)
Lena Ortiz: Draft runbook doc and circulate for review (due 2026-11-24)
next_steps: Schedule 60m e2e benchmark with PL and infra on 2026-11-23
Attach example request traces to runbook and link to dashboards
Decide fallback scoring weights in follow-up meeting (Lena to propose)
Share draft runbook in #runtime-ops and request oncall feedback
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Start: 09:30 PST
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz / Darius Chen / Priya Kapoor / Mateo Ruiz / Aisha Thompson / Alexei Morozov / Sanjay Patel / Jules Park

Summary (auto-gen): map out latency degradation scenarios, prioritize fallbacks, and create a runbook draft.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we've got an hour-ish, uh, 70 minutes on the calendar, so let's try and cover the detection matrix and then the runbook skeleton.
[00:00:15] Darius Chen: Quick note, I flagged this because the last two incidents had similar signatures — p99 up, CPU saturation on the runtime nodes, KV miss spikes.
[00:00:30] Priya Kapoor: Yep and to add, kernel fallback kicked in once, but it took longer than expected 'cause the KV cache was thrashing during compaction, so the prefix cache wasn't helping.
[00:00:45] Mateo Ruiz: there was also a network egress blip to the storage backend, so some of our big sequence requests saw repeated retries, which magnified latency.
[00:01:05] Jules Park: I'm seeing in support tickets customers report tokenization stalls too, can be mistaken for model slowness when it's actually upstream.
[00:01:22] Lena Ortiz: Good. Let's go use-case by use-case. First scenario: cold prefix + high QPS causing KV cache miss storm. Who wants to propose detection heuristics?
[00:01:40] Darius Chen: Metric-wise, KV cache miss rate > 15% for 30s combined with p99 latency > 1.2s for generation requests. Also watch for consecutive OOM-ish alloc errors in the kernel logs.
[00:01:58] Priya Kapoor: That's fine but for detection we should tag traces as cold-start if the kv_hit_ratio is < 0.5 within first N tokens, because otherwise you get false positives for small context flows.
[00:02:15] Aisha Thompson: Question — is 1.2s p99 a universal threshold? we have different SLAs for hosted vs dedicated.
[00:02:30] Lena Ortiz: Good call. We should have profile per deployment-mode: hosted p99 threshold 1.2s, dedicated tiers higher tolerance, say 1.6s, and private depends on contract. We'll capture that in the runbook.
[00:02:45] Sanjay Patel: Also remember that quantized model variants might have better latency but can hurt quality. So fallback ordering matters.
[00:02:58] Priya Kapoor: I want to propose the two-tier fallback: first switch to quantized variant of same model with adjusted batch size and preemptive KV warm-up; if that doesn't bring p95 down, fallback to smaller model family or cached generative responses.
[00:03:20] Darius Chen: Scoring note — we need a numerical score: latency impact (weight 0.5), quality delta (0.3), cost delta (0.2). That gives us a simple policy to choose fallback.
[00:03:38] Lena Ortiz: Can someone capture the scoring example?
[00:03:41] Mateo Ruiz: I'll take it — I'll write a short spreadsheet with example requests and scores.
[00:03:50] Jules Park: Also, don't forget to tie this into billing(??) signals — if cost spikes dramatically, ops will want to throttle.
[00:04:02] Lena Ortiz: Right. Next scenario: kernel fallback causing increased tail latency due to suboptimal kernels.
[00:04:16] Priya Kapoor: The kernel fallback path is safer but slower, especially for long sequences > 1024 tokens. We should detect run-time kernel switches using the kernel_id tag on traces. If kernel_switch_count > 3 in 60s, escalate.
[00:04:32] Darius Chen: We saw kernel switch storms during last deploy where a new kernel had a memory regression. Also watch for cgroups OOM and nvml memory pressure.
[00:04:47] Aisha Thompson: On the QA side I'll add synthetic tests to provoke kernel fallback and verify end-to-end latency does not regresses beyond threshold.
[00:04:58] Lena Ortiz: Great. For mitigation options here — quick fix is model variant fallback, better is to pull a canary off, right?
[00:05:12] Sanjay Patel: Yes, automated canary rollback should be the primary mitigation if the regression is correlated with a deploy tag.
[00:05:20] Lena Ortiz: Who owns canary rollback automation?
[00:05:23] Sanjay Patel: I do; we have existing hooks in release pipeline. I'll make sure the pipeline can trigger rollback when our telem alerts fire.
[00:05:30] Mateo Ruiz: We should also have an incrementally staged fallback — like reduce batch sizes, prioritize latency queues, then fallback to quantized model.
[00:05:43] Darius Chen: Note — reducing batch size increases per-token cost. If we do that automatically, include a cost limit per minute to avoid runaway spend.
[00:05:55] Lena Ortiz: Ok adding cost guard. Next: mem pressure and GPU OOMs causing tripped requests.
[00:06:10] Priya Kapoor: We saw this with larger context windows. Suggest a soft evict policy: if nvml memory > 90% for N seconds, drain low-priority workers and re-route high-priority traffic to a smaller model.
[00:06:25] Aisha Thompson: Also test for memory compaction side-effects; some compaction runs cause prolonged stalls. We'll annotate those maintenance windows.
[00:06:36] Darius Chen: In the detection matrix we should include kernel logs, nvml memory pressure, and per-GPU tail latency.
[00:06:46] Lena Ortiz: Let's pivot to runbook format. I want: Detection -> Initial Triage -> Mitigation -> Communication -> Postmortem triggers. Keep it one page if possible.
[00:07:02] Jules Park: Communication: For customer-impacting events we send an incident banner and notify CSMs. For internal-only latency blips, just post in #runtime-ops.
[00:07:15] Lena Ortiz: Agreed. Now walk through an example runbook entry: KV miss storm.
[00:07:22] Darius Chen: Detection: KV miss rate > X and p99 > Y. Initial triage: check KV node health and recent compaction jobs. If compaction running, pause compaction, trigger prewarm job.
[00:07:41] Priya Kapoor: Mitigation: 1) prewarm using prefix sampling; 2) reduce batch sizes for a short window; 3) fallback to quantized variant for affected routes.
[00:07:55] Mateo Ruiz: Also we can lift cached responses for deterministic endpoints as a temporary measure.
[00:08:03] Lena Ortiz: Who needs to be paged? Oncall + runtime oncall + release eng?
[00:08:10] Darius Chen: Page primary oncall + runtime SRE. If it's a deploy correlation, add release eng.
[00:08:16] Sanjay Patel: I'll add a script to the runbook to attach the last successful deploy hash and recent kernel version so triage is faster.
[00:08:27] Aisha Thompson: For postmortem triggers: if SLA breach > 4 hours or > 10% customer errors for > 30m then full postmortem.
[00:08:40] Lena Ortiz: Good. Telemetry gaps — what are we missing?
[00:08:44] Priya Kapoor: p99 tracing for cold-starts, kernel switch counters, CVR (cache-vs-request) breakouts, and a simple cold tag we can set on scheduler when prewarm hasn't run.
[00:09:00] Mateo Ruiz: Also we should capture the sequence length distribution in the request logs to see when long sequences correlate with slowdowns.
[00:09:11] Darius Chen: Sampling — we need more aggressive log sampling for the tail traces; currently we sample at 0.1% which misses these events.
[00:09:21] Lena Ortiz: Action: increase sampling to 1% for tail errors and add a noisy-log explosion guard, so we don't DDOS logging infra.
[00:09:33] Jules Park: People will worry about cost — make sure we justify the sampling increase with expected triage speed improvement.
[00:09:42] Lena Ortiz: On fallback ordering — recap: 1) reduce batch + prewarm, 2) quantized same-model, 3) smaller model family, 4) cached responses or degraded mode. Agree?
[00:09:58] Team: yes / yeah / agreed (crosstalk)
[00:10:15] Priya Kapoor: Clarify the prewarm signal: a scheduler API call that can be fired with a route and set of prefixes; it should try priming the kv cache asynchronously. We need an idempotent API.
[00:10:29] Mateo Ruiz: Implementation detail: scheduler should prioritize prewarm jobs with lower mem footprint and with special prewarm kernel to avoid interfering with production loads.
[00:10:40] Darius Chen: We'll also want a prewarm success metric: percent of prefetched prefixes that get hits within first M requests.
[00:10:50] Lena Ortiz: Who's building the prewarm API prototype?
[00:10:53] Darius Chen: I'll own the API + test harness.
[00:10:58] Aisha Thompson: I'll own the regression tests to validate it.
[00:11:05] Lena Ortiz: Great. Now fallback scoring weights we mentioned earlier — Darius will draft spreadsheet, Mateo will provide sample workloads.
[00:11:14] Mateo Ruiz: I'll prepare two workloads: one conversational (many short-turn requests) and one long-context summarization.
[00:11:24] Sanjay Patel: We should run the workloads against quantized variants and measure ROUGE/EM/perplexity or appropriate quality metrics, not just human judgement.
[00:11:36] Priya Kapoor: Also measure hallucination rate on the smaller models. Quality vs latency tradeoffs must be explicit.
[00:11:45] Lena Ortiz: Ok. Let's timebox the fallback weight decision to a follow-up next week.
[00:11:52] Darius Chen: On the subject of automated rollback — Sanjay will add a hook to monitor anomaly score and trigger rollback if score crosses threshold for N minutes.
[00:12:03] Sanjay Patel: Yes, but ensure we have safety: rollback should not cascade into tripping other alerts. We'll add a cooldown period.
[00:12:12] Lena Ortiz: Communication templates — Jules?
[00:12:15] Jules Park: I'll draft two templates: Customer-facing incident banner and internal triage note. Keep customer banner minimal: impact, affected routes, mitigation, ETA.
[00:12:28] Aisha Thompson: For internal note include links to traces, last deploy hash, kernel version, and memory graphs.
[00:12:36] Lena Ortiz: Telemetry dashboards — what's missing visually?
[00:12:40] Mateo Ruiz: Add a kernel events panel, prewarm hit rate, per-route p95/p99, and a compaction job timeline overlay.
[00:12:53] Darius Chen: Add an overlay for batch size changes and recent deploys so triage can correlate.
[00:12:59] Lena Ortiz: Great. Any objections to making the runbook the single source of truth?
[00:13:05] Team: no objections.
[00:13:10] Lena Ortiz: Ok time check — we've covered detection and mitigations; we need to agree on owners and two immediate engineering spikes: prewarm API + e2e bench. Anybody opposed?
[00:13:25] (brief silence)
[00:13:30] Darius Chen: Not opposed.
[00:13:32] Priya Kapoor: Fine.
[00:13:35] Lena Ortiz: Perfect. We'll also do a tabletop next Thursday with oncall to walk through runbook.
[00:13:42] Jules Park: I'll coordinate the tabletop and invite SRE, oncall and PL.
[00:13:47] Lena Ortiz: Ok let's go into a little technical deep-dive — Priya you mentioned kernel switch counters earlier, can you explain exactly how we instrument that?
[00:13:57] Priya Kapoor: Sure. At the runtime boundary we emit kernel_id and kernel_dispatch_time for each invocation. We can aggregate kernel_switch_count per host and per request id by counting distinct kernel_id sequence changes. We need to ensure we don't add too much tracing overhead.
[00:14:18] Mateo Ruiz: On the storage side, I'll add a small flag to compaction jobs so we can tell meltdowns caused by compaction vs normal growth.
[00:14:28] Darius Chen: Also consider tracking eviction reasons in KV metrics: memory_pressure vs ttl_expiry vs manual_compaction.
[00:14:39] Lena Ortiz: Good. Now let's simulate an example timeline for the runbook: detection at T+0, mitigation at T+4min, fallback at T+10min, rollback at T+18min if continues. Sound reasonable?
[00:14:54] Sanjay Patel: Yes but rollback window might be shorter for high-severity customer-impacting.
[00:15:02] Aisha Thompson: For HQ customers, set rollback at T+8min threshold.
[00:15:09] Lena Ortiz: Noted. Action items recap — Darius prewarm API, Priya fallback prototype, Mateo instrumentation, Aisha tests, Lena runbook doc.
[00:15:23] (crosstalk; people agreeing)
[00:15:30] Lena Ortiz: Anything else before we wrap?
[00:15:32] Jules Park: small thing — let's include an audit log requirement for fallback events, so security can review later.
[00:15:42] Darius Chen: We'll emit fallback events with actor (automated or manual), timestamp, and policy id.
[00:15:50] Lena Ortiz: Great. Alright team, meeting adjourn in a sec, but please update the action items in the doc. We'll reconvene next week to lock weights and review the benchmark results.
[00:16:05] End of main discussion.

Notes (auto):
- Transcript has some noise and mis-attribution; timestamps are approximate.
- References to a few product names were garbled in auto-transcribe (e.g., "KV cache" transcribed as "K-V cage" in some snippets).

Appendix: Short runbook snippet (one-line bullets for the doc):
- Detection: define per-mode p95/p99 thresholds, KV miss alarms, kernel_switch_count alerts.
- Initial triage: check recent deploy, kernel versions, compaction jobs, storage latency.
- Mitigation: prewarm -> reduce batch -> quantized fallback -> smaller model -> cache responses.
- Communication: issue incident banner if customers impacted; internal post in #runtime-ops otherwise.
- Postmortem triggers: prolonged SLA breach or >10% errors for >30m.

End of transcript.
